GPX file guide

How to get a GPX file with the timestamps your photos need.

Record the outing with an iPhone app or GPS watch, finish the activity, then export the recorded track as GPX. A planned route or a line downloaded from a map may look correct but often has no timestamps.

The short answer

Use a recording, not a route plan.

Use this

Recorded activity or track

  • GPS points collected while you were there
  • Each usable point includes its time
  • Covers the period when photos were taken
Usually not enough

Planned route or course

  • May contain only a line to follow
  • Often has no original timestamps
  • Cannot prove where you were at photo time
Do not judge a GPX file by the map preview.

For photo geotagging, the useful file contains track points such as <trkpt> with a <time> value. A beautiful route line without time cannot place a photo on the trip.

Choose what you already carry

Four practical ways to create the file.

IPHONE

Record with a phone app

Strava is the simplest familiar option. OsmAnd, Gaia GPS, and Guru Maps are useful when offline maps or direct file export matter.

Compare iPhone recording apps →
APPLE WATCH

Record without carrying the phone

Use Strava or WorkOutDoors on the watch, or sync a native Apple Workout through Strava before exporting it.

See Apple Watch methods →
GPS WATCH

Export an outdoor activity

Garmin Connect, the COROS app, and the Suunto app can export a recorded outdoor activity as GPX.

Open watch export steps →
SHARED TRIP

Ask for the original activity file

If someone else logged the trip, ask them for the GPX export of the recorded workout—not a screenshot, public map link, or planned course.

Before the first photo

Set up a continuous, believable timeline.

  1. Turn on automatic date and timeKeep the iPhone, watch, and camera clocks as close as possible. LensPin can correct a fixed camera offset later, but a correct start is easier to review.
  2. Allow precise location and background recordingGrant the recording app the permissions it needs before leaving. Test it outdoors once rather than discovering a permission problem after the trip.
  3. Wait for a stable GPS positionStart outside with a clear view of the sky. Begin recording before the first camera photo and finish after the last one.
  4. Prefer one continuous activityFor photo matching, leaving auto-pause off can make long stops and short walks easier to understand. If you pause manually, remember that the gap remains a real evidence boundary.
  5. Save the activity before opening LensPinLet the device finish syncing, export the recorded activity as .gpx, and keep the original file unchanged.

A 30-second file check

Confirm that you exported the right thing.

CheckGood signWarning sign
File nameEnds in .gpxA screenshot, PDF, share link, ZIP, or route-only file
Track timeThe activity details show the day and duration of the photo outingThe route has distance but no recorded start time
Map coverageThe line covers the places and period in which you photographedThe line stops early, starts late, or jumps between distant places
LensPin importTimed track points and continuous segments are detected“No timed track points” or no coverage near the photo time
